quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: ____ it costs more, I'm booking the flight with better legroom for such a long trip.
quests.sentence: ____ it costs more, I'm booking the flight with better legroom for such a long trip.
quests.hint: The decision stays the same no matter what happens with the price - that's stronger than a simple condition.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' shows the decision holds regardless of whether the cost turns out higher. 'If' alone would suggest the decision purely depends on the cost, without that 'regardless' sense.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - even if (outcome unaffected by the condition)

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: The marathon organizers will hold the race as scheduled ____ the weather forecast turns unfavorable overnight.
quests.sentence: The marathon organizers will hold the race as scheduled ____ the weather forecast turns unfavorable overnight.
quests.hint: The race happens regardless of what the weather does - not depending on it, and not only in the absence of bad weather.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' shows the race goes ahead no matter what the weather does. 'Unless' would incorrectly suggest bad weather could actually cancel the race.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: ____ nobody else believes your idea, I'll always support you.
quests.sentence: ____ nobody else believes your idea, I'll always support you.
quests.hint: This support holds true no matter what other people think - the strongest possible version of a condition.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' emphasizes that the support doesn't depend on others' opinions at all. 'If' alone would suggest support is conditional on that specific situation, missing the 'no matter what' sense.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ it was pouring rain outside, the kids insisted on playing in the yard.
quests.sentence: ____ it was pouring rain outside, the kids insisted on playing in the yard.
quests.hint: This describes something that actually happened - the rain was real, not just a possibility.
quests.explanation: 'Even though' fits because the rain was an actual, factual situation. 'Even if' would only work for a hypothetical rain that might or might not happen.
quests.grammarRule: Concession vs Condition - even though (factual), not even if (hypothetical)

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: ____ it starts pouring rain during the game, the referees plan to keep playing unless there's lightning.
quests.sentence: ____ it starts pouring rain during the game, the referees plan to keep playing unless there's lightning.
quests.hint: The rain hasn't happened yet here - this is about a possible future situation, not something already true.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' fits this hypothetical, not-yet-happened situation. 'Even though' would only work if the rain were already a real, current fact.
quests.grammarRule: Condition vs Concession - even if (hypothetical), not even though (factual)

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: ____ the market crashes next month, Sofia plans to keep contributing to her retirement fund every paycheck.
quests.sentence: ____ the market crashes next month, Sofia plans to keep contributing to her retirement fund every paycheck.
quests.hint: The market crash is only a possible future event here, not something that has already happened.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' fits this hypothetical future scenario. 'Even though' would only be correct if the crash had already occurred.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: ____ the client rejects this draft, we'll simply revise it and try again - we're not worried either way.
quests.sentence: ____ the client rejects this draft, we'll simply revise it and try again - we're not worried either way.
quests.hint: The phrase 'either way' tells you the reaction doesn't change based on the outcome - that's stronger than a simple condition.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' matches the 'either way' attitude - staying calm no matter what happens. Plain 'if' would just describe the condition without that added sense of indifference to the outcome.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - even if vs if (added emphasis on indifference to outcome)

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ the venue is available next Saturday, we'll book it for the reunion.
quests.sentence: ____ the venue is available next Saturday, we'll book it for the reunion.
quests.hint: The booking simply depends on availability - there's no sense of 'no matter what' here.
quests.explanation: 'If' introduces this simple, straightforward condition. 'Even if' would incorrectly add an unnecessary sense of 'regardless,' which doesn't fit this plain booking decision.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - if (plain condition, no added emphasis)

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: Maria promised to pick up her daughter from practice ____ she has to leave work early to do it.
quests.sentence: Maria promised to pick up her daughter from practice ____ she has to leave work early to do it.
quests.hint: The promise holds true no matter what inconvenience it causes her - a stronger commitment than a simple condition would suggest.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' emphasizes her commitment regardless of the inconvenience. 'Unless' would incorrectly suggest leaving work early might cancel her plan instead of being something she's willing to do anyway.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: ____ you finish your vegetables, you can have dessert.
quests.sentence: ____ you finish your vegetables, you can have dessert.
quests.hint: This sets up a clear requirement that must be met - a slightly firmer, rule-like condition.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' introduces this requirement with a firmer, rule-like feel than a plain 'if' would carry, though 'if' would also work here. 'Because' would incorrectly frame this as an explanation rather than a condition.

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: Tenants can keep pets in the apartment ____ the pets don't cause damage to the property.
quests.sentence: Tenants can keep pets in the apartment ____ the pets don't cause damage to the property.
quests.hint: This sets a clear ongoing requirement that must continue to be true for pets to be allowed.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' expresses this ongoing requirement clearly. 'If' would also work but doesn't carry quite the same sense of a continuing condition that must keep holding true.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ you deliver the project by the agreed date, the client won't mind which hours you work.
quests.sentence: ____ you deliver the project by the agreed date, the client won't mind which hours you work.
quests.hint: The flexibility on hours depends entirely on meeting this one requirement - the deadline.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' sets the deadline as the key requirement for flexibility elsewhere. 'Unless' would reverse the framing, suggesting flexibility disappears only if the deadline isn't met, which doesn't match the positive requirement being described here.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: You can freeze your membership for up to three months ____ you notify the gym in writing beforehand.
quests.sentence: You can freeze your membership for up to three months ____ you notify the gym in writing beforehand.
quests.hint: Notifying in writing is presented as a clear requirement here - a firm prerequisite, not just a loose possibility.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' fits this firm, ongoing requirement well. 'If' would also work, but sounds slightly less like an official condition of the policy.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - as long as (firm requirement) vs if (general condition)

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: ____ you're free Saturday, want to grab lunch together?
quests.sentence: ____ you're free Saturday, want to grab lunch together?
quests.hint: This is a casual, simple question about availability - not a formal requirement or condition being set.
quests.explanation: 'If' fits this casual, simple question naturally. 'As long as' would sound oddly formal or demanding for a relaxed lunch invitation.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - if (casual) vs as long as (more like a firm requirement)

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: The daycare will continue watching your child after 6pm ____ you call ahead to let them know.
quests.sentence: The daycare will continue watching your child after 6pm ____ you call ahead to let them know.
quests.hint: Calling ahead is presented as a clear, ongoing requirement for this extended service.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' fits this firm requirement well. 'If' would also technically work, but 'as long as' better matches the sense of an official policy condition.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ all parties agree to the revised terms, the contract can be finalized by Friday.
quests.sentence: ____ all parties agree to the revised terms, the contract can be finalized by Friday.
quests.hint: This sounds like formal contract language - which of these phrases fits that register best?
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' is a formal way of saying 'if,' fitting this contract-like context well. 'If' would also work but sounds noticeably less formal.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: Students may retake the exam once ____ they submit a formal request within two weeks of the results.
quests.sentence: Students may retake the exam once ____ they submit a formal request within two weeks of the results.
quests.hint: This reads like an official policy statement - the more formal condition phrase fits best here.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' suits this formal, official tone. 'If' would also technically work but feels less suited to this precise policy language.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: ____ the applicant meets the minimum income requirement, the visa will be processed within thirty days.
quests.sentence: ____ the applicant meets the minimum income requirement, the visa will be processed within thirty days.
quests.hint: This is written in formal, official language - the more formal condition phrase fits this register.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' matches this formal, bureaucratic tone. 'Unless' would reverse the logic, suggesting the visa is processed only when the requirement isn't met.

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: ____ you're not too tired, want to watch another episode?
quests.sentence: ____ you're not too tired, want to watch another episode?
quests.hint: This is a relaxed, casual question - the more formal condition phrase would sound oddly stiff here.
quests.explanation: 'If' fits this casual, everyday question naturally. 'Provided that' would sound unnecessarily formal for such a relaxed invitation.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: The vendor will honor the discounted rate ____ the order is placed before the end of the month.
quests.sentence: The vendor will honor the discounted rate ____ the order is placed before the end of the month.
quests.hint: This reads like formal business correspondence - the more formal condition phrase fits this tone.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' suits this formal business context well. 'If' would also technically work but feels a touch less suited to this precise, official register.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: ____ the policyholder reports the incident within 48 hours, the claim will be processed under standard terms.
quests.sentence: ____ the policyholder reports the incident within 48 hours, the claim will be processed under standard terms.
quests.hint: This is formal insurance policy language - the more formal condition phrase fits this register.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' matches this formal, official tone well. 'Unless' would reverse the meaning, suggesting the claim is processed only when the report isn't made in time.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: Employees can work from home two days a week ____ their productivity doesn't drop.
quests.sentence: Employees can work from home two days a week ____ their productivity doesn't drop.
quests.hint: This is another formal way of stating a condition, just like 'provided that.'
quests.explanation: 'Providing that' works exactly like 'provided that,' introducing a formal condition. 'If' would also work but sounds less official.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - providing that (same as provided that)

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: The festival organizers confirmed the event will proceed ____ ticket sales fall short of last year's numbers.
quests.sentence: The festival organizers confirmed the event will proceed ____ ticket sales fall short of last year's numbers.
quests.hint: The event happens regardless of ticket sales - not depending on hitting a certain number.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' shows the event proceeds no matter what happens with ticket sales. 'If' alone would suggest the event's fate actually depends on the sales numbers.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ you spend at least fifty dollars this month, you'll automatically earn double reward points.
quests.sentence: ____ you spend at least fifty dollars this month, you'll automatically earn double reward points.
quests.hint: This is formal promotional language stating a clear condition for the reward.
quests.explanation: 'Providing that' introduces this formal condition clearly. 'Unless' would reverse the logic, suggesting points are earned only when the spending requirement isn't met.

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: The account will be closed automatically ____ you make at least one transaction this year.
quests.sentence: The account will be closed automatically ____ you make at least one transaction this year.
quests.hint: Closure happens specifically when a transaction does NOT occur - which connector already includes that 'not'?
quests.explanation: 'Unless' shows the account stays open only if a transaction happens; otherwise it's closed. 'If' would need 'don't make' added to express the same meaning.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: ____ the bakery had never made a wedding cake before, they agreed to take on the challenge.
quests.sentence: ____ the bakery had never made a wedding cake before, they agreed to take on the challenge.
quests.hint: Taking on this challenge despite no prior experience is the unexpected twist here.
quests.explanation: 'Although' shows the concession between their lack of experience and their willingness to try anyway. 'If' would incorrectly turn this into a hypothetical rather than an actual decision they made.

quests.instruction: Select the connector that best completes the sentence.
quests.question: The coach benched the star player ____ he'd missed practice three times without an excuse.
quests.sentence: The coach benched the star player ____ he'd missed practice three times without an excuse.
quests.hint: This explains the actual reason for the decision, which already happened - not a hypothetical condition.
quests.explanation: 'Because' gives the real, factual reason behind the benching. 'If' would incorrectly suggest this was a hypothetical situation rather than something that had already occurred.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that fits best.
quests.question: ____ the shipment arrives a few days late, we've built enough buffer into the schedule to avoid missing the launch date.
quests.sentence: ____ the shipment arrives a few days late, we've built enough buffer into the schedule to avoid missing the launch date.
quests.hint: The launch date is protected no matter what happens with the shipment timing, not simply dependent on it arriving on time.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' captures this 'no matter what' sense about a possible delay. 'As long as' or 'provided that' would instead suggest the timing must meet a specific requirement, which isn't the buffer-protected situation described here.
quests.grammarRule: Condition - even if vs as long as / provided that

quests.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best connector.
quests.question: The scholarship will be renewed each year ____ the student maintains a minimum GPA of 3.0.
quests.sentence: The scholarship will be renewed each year ____ the student maintains a minimum GPA of 3.0.
quests.hint: Maintaining the GPA is an ongoing requirement that must continue being true each year, not just a one-time possibility.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' fits this continuing, year-after-year requirement well. 'If' would also technically work but doesn't emphasize the requirement needing to keep holding true over time as clearly.

quests.instruction: Choose the connector that correctly links the two clauses.
quests.question: New members can join the committee at any point in the year ____ they attend an orientation session first.
quests.sentence: New members can join the committee at any point in the year ____ they attend an orientation session first.
quests.hint: Attending orientation is presented here as an official, formal prerequisite for joining.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' introduces this formal prerequisite clearly. 'Unless' would reverse the framing, suggesting joining is blocked only when orientation isn't attended, rather than presenting it as a requirement to fulfill.
